newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Bombs kill five, wound 50 in Algiers before poll.
newsitem.headline: Bombs kill five, wound 50 in Algiers before poll.

text.p: Two bombs exploded in Algiers on Sunday, killing five people, wounding about 50 and bringing fear to the capital just days before a general election, witnesses and residents said.
The election, due on Thursday, is meant to end over five years of bloodshed, including countless bombings.
Eyewitnesses said one bomb ripped through a crowded bus just before it was to leave Martyrs' Square in the heart of the city to take workers home around 4 p.m. (1500 GMT).
"It was full of workers heading home and the bomb went off just before it left the bus station," one witness said.
Police quickly ringed the area as ambulances, sirens screaming, raced to and from the scene, bathed in bright sunlight.

Security forces said the bomb attack, which they termed a "criminal act" -- official shorthand for attacks by Moslem fundamentalists -- had killed five, including a baby, and wounded at least 16, according to preliminary estimates.
Witnesses said they thought about 30 people had been caught by the blast and wounded.

Bombs have killed hundreds of people and wounded thousands in the conflict between Moslem rebels and security forces, and early this year Algiers city authorities brought in draconian parking measures to try to thwart car bombs.

More than 200,000 troops and security forces are expected to be deployed nationwide for Thursday's parliamentary election to protect the nearly 18 million registered voters. But residents said there few obvious signs so far of extra security in the capital.
Witnesses said the second bomb went off in Gharmoul Street, in another part of the city centre, wounding between 15 and 20 people.
The street houses the headquarters of the civil protection service, responsible for rescue work in such attacks. The blast was heard 1.5 km away by guests in the Aurassi Hotel.
There have been fears of increasing violence in the runup to Thursday's election which Algerian authorities hope will help end the years of bloodshed they blame on Moslem fundamentalists.
Algeria has been without a parliament since the authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election in which the radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had taken a commanding first round lead.

Violence erupted shortly afterwards and about 60,000 people have been killed. A series of massacres in isolated villages, with scores of people including children having their throats cut, have marked the runup to the election campaigning.
On Saturday, a bomb exploded in a cinema in the Algerian capital. Officials said five people were wounded, two seriously. An Algerian newspaper on Sunday put the toll at one dead and 24 wounded.
